title: Reading 4: Innovation systems for transformations towards sustainability? Taking the normative dimension seriously

chapters.title: The paper in brief
paragraphs: The paper asks how the innovation systems framework can support transformations towards sustainability (page 1). Humanity faces multiple crises, and Rockström and colleagues claim that several planetary boundaries have already been crossed. Such wicked problems have emergent, socially embedded causes and uncertain effects. Technological solutions alone will not suffice, the authors argue; wicked problems call for transformations in economic, institutional, technical, cultural and organizational dimensions (page 2).

The central claim is that this needs a paradigm shift. In the current paradigm, innovation is seen as per se desirable and mostly technological (page 1). Following Niosi and colleagues, an innovation system is a system of interacting agents aiming at the production of science and technology, whose interaction serves its development, protection, financing or regulation (page 2). On page 4, a paradigm is a set of assumptions, concepts, values and practices that make up a worldview and span a bounded performative space, with feedback loops between paradigm and practice. The authors call the alternative a dedicated innovation system, a term from Pyka, here dedicated to transformations towards sustainability. Table 1 on page 5 contrasts the two paradigms: economic growth, efficiency and system improvement against continuity of ecological systems, justice between and within generations, and quality of life. Dedicated systems add transformative innovation, which Steward calls paradigm-breaking, system-wide novelty, and policies against what Weber and Rohracher call transformational failures.

Three questions follow (pages 5 to 7). Directionality asks what to transform or sustain. Legitimacy asks why, and who decides. Responsibility asks by and for whom. Each is hard. Debates on direction often assume we already know the right direction, which clashes with open-ended evolutionary processes and conflicting interests. Top-down steering is futile in a network society, yet bottom-up participation cannot guarantee the right solutions either. Corporate social responsibility and liability do not fit collective, uncertain outcomes (page 7).

The method is a conceptual synthesis. The authors review building blocks: transformative innovation policy, innovation systems foresight, the entrepreneurial state, green industrial policy, inclusive innovation systems, reflexive governance, transitions research and responsible innovation (pages 7 to 9). Their verdict is that these strands are scattered, and that only a shift to the paradigm level can integrate the normativity of sustainability (page 10). A dedicated system can in principle subordinate innovation trajectories to a sustainability goal. The paper ends with nine open research questions, from resistance to change and leverage points to shared responsibility, stakeholder selection, and differences in space and time (pages 9 and 10). It names no limitations of its own, but closes with Sendzimir and colleagues' reminder that no analysis will ever eliminate surprise and uncertainty.

In the course, the paper is used most in Lecture 1, Innovation as systemic and sustainable transformation, whose fourth part builds on pages 1, 3, 6 and 7. Lecture 2 brings it back for regional innovation systems, and Lecture 9 shows it on slide 27. Among its eight authors are Jan Fagerberg, of Reading 1, and Allan Dahl Andersen, of Reading 10. In our own reading, it helps with Question 1 of December 2024, which asks what you understand by innovation system, sustainable transformation, agency and institutions. Here is an example of our own, not from the paper: a regional system that funds every new technology alike has no direction; asking what to change, who decides and who answers for the result turns it towards sustainability.

checks.q: What shift in perspective do the authors call for in this paper?
checks.a: A paradigm shift: from conventional innovation systems, which treat innovation as per se desirable and mostly technological, to innovation systems dedicated to transformations towards sustainability.

checks.q: What three core normative questions must dedicated innovation systems address according to the authors?
checks.a: Directionality (what to transform or keep), legitimacy (why and who decides), and responsibility (by and for whom).

chapters.title: Introduction and the limits of conventional innovation systems
paragraphs: The abstract states the aim: to complement research on transformations towards sustainability with the innovation systems framework. In the current paradigm, innovations are seen as per se desirable and mostly technological, so the authors call for a paradigm shift towards systems dedicated to sustainability, with research on directionality, legitimacy and responsibility. Among the eight authors are Fagerberg and Andersen. The introduction lists multiple crises, from climate change to the unjust distribution of wealth. Rockström and colleagues claim that planetary boundaries have been crossed, and such wicked problems have emergent, socially embedded causes and uncertain effects.

Because sustainability is deeply normative, technological solutions will not suffice, and wicked problems call for transformations in economic, institutional, technical, cultural and organizational dimensions. The authors aim to discuss the missing normative dimension of innovation systems and argue for a paradigm shift. Innovation systems grew from evolutionary economics as a challenge to neoclassical economics. Following Niosi and colleagues, they are systems of interacting agents aiming at the production of science and technology, whose interaction serves its development, protection, financing or regulation. The framework informs research, policy and firms, and has been applied at national, regional, sectoral and technological levels.

Page 3 highlights the limits of conventional innovation systems when confronting sustainability. For decades, innovation research has suffered from a pro-innovation bias, assuming innovation is per se desirable. Existing sustainability-oriented approaches focus narrowly on solving environmental problems through technological solutions. The authors argue this is insufficient. Transformations towards sustainability require changing routines, practices and habits of producers and consumers, embracing institutional and cultural changes. Because sustainability is not merely a technical optimization puzzle, innovation systems research must explicitly address the normative goals and desirability of innovation processes.

checks.q: What inherent fallacy in innovation research do the authors identify on page 3?
checks.a: The assumption that innovation is per se desirable, which overlooks the ethical acceptability and societal desirability of innovations.

checks.q: How do the authors define an innovation system on page 2 citing Niosi and colleagues?
checks.a: Systems of interacting agents aiming at the production of science and technology, whose interaction serves its development, protection, financing or regulation.

chapters.title: The normative dimension and dedicated innovation systems
paragraphs: Firms such as Unilever and Shell see a sustainable society differently from Greenpeace, so presuming consensus is a mistake. The authors therefore shift attention to the paradigm level. A paradigm is a set of assumptions, concepts, values and practices that make up a worldview and span a bounded performative space; paradigm and practice shape each other through feedback loops. Following Pyka, they call the alternative a dedicated innovation system, here dedicated to transformations towards sustainability. Early innovation systems aimed at economic development, but today innovation is treated as an aim in itself, with economic growth and efficiency as dominant values.

Page 5 compares conventional and dedicated innovation system frameworks. Following Renn and colleagues, sustainability norms include ecological continuity, intergenerational and intragenerational justice, and quality of life. Table 1 contrasts the two frameworks. While conventional systems focus on supply-side technological innovation and traditional system failures, dedicated systems emphasize transformative innovation, following Steward, and transformational failures, following Weber and Rohracher. Dedicating systems to sustainability requires answering three central questions: transform or sustain what, why, and by and for whom.

Directionality asks what to transform or keep, opening diverse pathways while closing unsustainable ones. Debates often assume we already know the right direction, which is questionable for wicked problems: direction-setting clashes with open-ended evolutionary processes, as the German Advisory Council on Global Change notes, and consensus is unlikely. Legitimacy asks why a goal is desirable and who decides. Top-down steering is futile in a network society, yet bottom-up participation cannot guarantee the right solutions, and grassroots movements need critical mass. Values and paradigms, many argue, are shaped by cultural evolution.

checks.q: What three central questions must a dedicated innovation system address according to page 5?
checks.a: Transform or sustain what, why, and by and for whom.

checks.q: Why is setting directionality difficult in an evolutionary system according to page 6?
checks.a: Because transformations are open-ended processes with uncertain results, and wicked problems involve multiple actors with conflicting interests.

chapters.title: Responsibility, building blocks and the research agenda
paragraphs: Responsibility asks by and for whom, linking agency with power and consequences. Corporate social responsibility and liability do not fit collective processes with unknown causalities, so neither individual nor collective responsibility concepts are entirely suitable. To sum up, transformations can be analysed with an innovation systems framework, but only after a paradigm change that engages with directionality, legitimacy and responsibility. Section 4 turns to building blocks: agreements from the Kyoto Protocol to the Sustainable Development Goals show that setting goals is easier than directing innovation. Transformative innovation policies aim to steer socio-technical systems in socially desirable directions.

Page 8 reviews frameworks that create goal-orientation and legitimacy. Innovation systems foresight, from Andersen and Andersen, builds participatory visions for system change. Mazzucato highlights the entrepreneurial state, while Rodrik advocates distributed green industrial policy. Inclusive innovation systems focus on lower-income groups, and Bryden and Gezelius combine innovation systems with human rights and triple bottom line accounting. Lindner and colleagues suggest reflexive governance. Proponents of sustainability transitions research, applied in the Netherlands and Belgium, provide operational frameworks like transition management, strategic niche management and transition arenas.

Responsible innovation, following Arnaldi and colleagues, steers innovation from the inside towards societal goals, and Lubberink and colleagues name six dimensions, such as anticipation, reflexivity and deliberation. The building blocks are scattered, so the main question is how dedicated innovation systems can incorporate legitimate goal-orientation for transformative innovation by and for society. Seven open questions follow on this page: systemic resistance to change, multiple pathways, places to intervene, a systemic concept of responsibility, responsibility as shared and tied to power, policies against transformational failures, and how to encourage participation and select the right stakeholders.

checks.q: What central question for future research do the authors propose on page 9?
checks.a: How dedicated innovation systems can incorporate legitimate goal-orientation for transformative innovation by and for society.

checks.q: Why are traditional concepts of responsibility insufficient for innovation systems on page 7?
checks.a: Because complex systems involve unknown causalities, unintended consequences, and outcomes resulting from combined individual and collective action.

chapters.title: Conclusions and the reference list
paragraphs: Two more questions close the agenda: which elements of dedicated systems are universal or contingent, and how systems differ in time. Citing Sendzimir and colleagues, researchers must engage uncertainty as a stimulus rather than a basis for apathy. The conclusions say the current framework focuses too much on technology and treats innovation as per se desirable, so shifting attention to the paradigm level is the only way to integrate the normativity of sustainability. A dedicated system can in principle subordinate innovation trajectories to a sustainability goal.
These pages are the reference list.

checks.q: What main conclusion do the authors reach regarding the conventional innovation systems framework on page 10?
checks.a: It is insufficient for sustainability transformations because it focuses excessively on technological solutions and assumes innovation is per se desirable.
